title: pottery studio site (node-web, 9 units, MULTI-PAGE: shared layout + routing + per-item pages + a form)
provenance: LA direction 2026-08-06, verbatim: 'my current priority is for it to be able to engineer relatively complex website with multiple pages... We don't need to one-shot websites any more.' Authored because NO multi-page card existed: B3 and B5 are the only web cards and both ask for 'a page' - singular. A capability nothing measures cannot be iterated toward.
goal: I run a small pottery studio and I want a proper little website for it, not just one page. There should be a home page that introduces the studio, a page listing the pieces I have for sale, a separate page for each individual piece with its own details and photo, and a contact page where someone can send me an enquiry. Every page needs the same heading and menu across the top so it feels like one website and I can get anywhere from anywhere. The list of pieces and each piece's own page have to come from the same saved information, so when I change a piece's price it changes everywhere it appears. The contact page should keep the enquiries somewhere I can look at later, and it should tell someone politely if they have left something out instead of just losing what they typed. I would also like the piece list to let me narrow down to just the mugs or just the bowls.

expected_outcome.notes: THE MULTI-PAGE CARD. What this exercises that B3 and B5 cannot, because both of those build ONE page: (1) a SHARED LAYOUT - one header/nav rendered on four routes, so a change in one place must hold everywhere and cannot be copy-pasted per page; (2) ROUTING across four distinct routes including a PARAMETERISED one (per-piece detail), which is the first time the fleet must build a route it cannot enumerate at author time; (3) ONE data source feeding two different views (the list and the detail page), so a price change must propagate - the classic place a coder writes two sources of truth and both pass their own unit tests; (4) a FORM with validation that must PRESERVE the operator's typed text on rejection (the lesson-321 class, live at #1117 and #1168 on the operator's own surfaces - here it is graded rather than hoped for); (5) FILTERING that is behaviourally checkable without eyeballs. Visual criteria stay eyeball-tier and are rendered honestly UNVERIFIED, never auto-passed - unchanged from B3/B5, and the reason the visual-automation gap is worth closing separately rather than pretended away here. UNITS ARE CAPPED AT 8, NOT CHOSEN: decompose.py DEFAULT_MAX_TASKS = 8 and nothing on the dispatch path overrides it, so a 9th unit would be silently dropped with a 'plan capped at 8 tasks' warning. The four pages, the shared layout, the shared data source, the filtering and the acceptance tests fit in 8 exactly -- but the cap, not the product, is what set the number, and a genuinely larger site cannot be expressed as a single card until that cap moves. Budget: this card is intended for DEDICATED runs of one or two jobs, not the six-card set - per verify-battery-budget-coherence.ps1 C3, a global budget bump breaks the PT16H ceiling while a single long job fits comfortably.

run_budget_note: 8 h = CARD_RUN_BUDGET_MAX_S, the clamp ceiling. EXTRAPOLATED, NOT MEASURED: B3's own run_budget_note records node/web tasks measuring 40-85 minutes EACH on its first campaign run (5 tasks + gates + acceptance = 4.5-6.5 h), and B3 now carries 21600. B9 is a wider 8-unit multi-page card, so 6 h would likely repeat B3's stall. Without a declared budget a card falls to _DEFAULT_RUN_BUDGET_S = 10800 (3 h) -- the exact default B3 STALLED on -- which is why this is declared rather than left to inherit. Re-measure after the first real run and replace this note with the figure.
